items.title: ‘Chilling’: As Nepal Grapples With Flooding Chaos, Christians Face Another Potential Horror
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Pray.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Nepal deals with the horrific toll of tragic flooding that killed more than 1,000 people, at least 20 churches have reportedly been destroyed by the damaging waters.

Joel Veldkamp, head of international communications at Christian Solidarity International (CSI), told CBN News that one congregation has 80 individuals and families who lost their homes — and that’s just one example.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

CSI has been working to get food, mattresses, mosquito nets, cleaning supplies, and other items to people in Nepal to help meet basic needs.

Veldkamp said there’s another dynamic unfolding inside the South Asian nation: persecution, an issue gaining steam and attention before the deadly flooding began.

“We’ve seen in the last 10 years … persecution of Christians has spiked in Nepal,” he said. “It wasn’t really a big problem before, and today it’s still not on the scale like we’ll see in India, or Pakistan, or other nearby countries. But there is now a law against conversion, so it’s illegal to try to get someone else to change their religion.”

Veldkamp said this is a violation of human rights standards, but that this law is used to prosecute pastors and missionaries — even Christians who might happen to visit and speak with Hindu friends.

“We have seen an uptick in these cases of Christians being jailed on accusations,” he said, noting that sharing the Gospel can be enough to spark legal chaos.

Veldkamp said there’s a new government in Nepal after the previous regime was overthrown in a revolution. An election unfolded in March, which has only added to the uncertainty.

“We still don’t know really what that means, but the country is in flux [and] is headed in a new political direction,” he said. “There are some good signs and some bad signs from the new government, so Christians in Nepal are very concerned about which way the country is going to go now.”

Nepal is one of two Hindu-majority nations in the world, with India joining it in that distinction. Until 2008, Nepal was a Hindu nation before becoming a federal republic. Today, there are new calls to return to that previous designation — something that should be of concern to Christians and other religious minorities.

India has been reportedly putting pressure on Nepal to embrace Hindu nationalism, funding groups that seek to push Christians to reconvert, among other issues.

“There are serious efforts to change Nepal’s constitution to make it officially a Hindu country again,” Veldkamp said. “And in the current environment, that would mean probably the harassment of Christians. Attacks on churches would only increase because then it would be official that this country does not belong to Christians.”

With pastors, missionaries, and Christians already under fire, he said there’s a “real threat that is having a chilling effect” on believers in Nepal.

“Right now, when these things happen to Christians, Christians can say, ‘Hey, we’re a secular country. Nepal is a country for everyone. It says so in our Constitution,'” Veldkamp said. “And that’s … a good argument. That’s a good lever that they can use to appeal to their fellow Nepali citizens for justice.”

But if Nepal becomes a Hindu nation, these arguments dissipate both legally and in the public sphere. Veldkamp encouraged believers worldwide to pray for the church.

items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: SEU Worship Has a Question About Worship Music: Where Did the Joy Go?
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album. The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless. “I nee
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album.

The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless.

“I need a fully produced-out track at the end of a writing session,” she said. “I don’t have much vision up here when it comes to, like, man, this acoustic track — I’m just not sure how it lands.”

So when the group sat down early in the year to sort through what might make the record, Plank didn’t put it forward. Other people did.

“They were like, let’s just try this out,” she said. “And it has actually been the anthem of my heart now.”

It’s also the song with her name on it. “The Cost Is a Joy” is credited to SEU Worship and Chelsea Plank, and it hands Found in the Field — the group’s new live album, out now — both its argument and its title.

The argument started with something Shuffit had been noticing in Southeastern University’s students. He came up through the school himself before joining staff, and he prefaced the thought carefully.

“This is no shade towards anyone,” he said, at which point Plank cut in: “Gosh, I don’t know what he’s about to say.”

“There is a lot of language around the cost of following Jesus,” he continued. “The suffering of it, the hardship of it. And we just thought it was a fresh and important perspective for our students to have — that yes, there is suffering, but there is joy in this.”

Plank grew up on that language too, and she doesn’t think it’s wrong.

“It is such a powerful message,” she said. “Even when you hear David talking about, I’m not going to give the Lord an offering that costs me nothing. There is a price to following Jesus. It’s your whole life.”

The problem is what happens when the price is all anyone sings about.

“It can turn really legalistic really quick,” she said.

Her alternative puts the events in a different order. The surrender doesn’t come first and the joy doesn’t arrive later as a reward for it — the seeing comes first, and the giving-up follows from it almost as a reflex. “Out of the abundance of our heart of seeing him, of needing to know him — that’s easy. I will give up everything, and the cost is a joy.”

She has a line for this: “The kingdom of heaven is made up of righteousness, peace and joy. Joy is a third of the kingdom. Joy is the serious business of heaven, we like to say.”

The album title comes from the same place — the parable in Matthew where the kingdom is a treasure buried in a field, and the man who finds it sells everything he owns to buy the land. The transaction only makes sense if you know what’s in the ground. Not, as Plank puts it, “a begrudging act of surrender, but a joyful act of servitude.”

There’s a second reading of the phrase she likes as much: being found in the field of God’s presence, and staying there. “Giving up everything to remain there.”

Made for One Room

None of these songs arrived as an album. They arrived as chapel services.

SEU Worship is the worship movement at Southeastern University, an Assemblies of God school in Lakeland, Florida, and the group’s records are assembled backward from what already works in the room. Songs get played on campus for months before anyone decides whether they’re worth recording.

“When you hear an album of ours, usually we’ve been playing it all year on our campus,” Plank said. “It’s almost like a yearbook of our year. A snapshot of our year.”

“We play them on campus first to see if they even resonate with our community, or if they even work. And then what’s working in chapel and in our community is usually what makes the records every time.”

It’s a filter that runs in the opposite direction from most of the industry, where a song is written to travel and then handed to a congregation. Plank’s advice to other churches making music is to stop reaching so far.

“It is first and foremost for your community,” she said. “Who did God call you to steward? I can’t steward the nation. I can’t disciple the world.”

Even the writing sessions start there: “What’s the language that our community is missing? What concept do you feel like we’re needing to sing about?”

Rooms That Used to Be Empty

That approach got tested this summer, when SEU Worship — coming off a 10-day outpouring on campus in February that drew national attention — took songs written for one chapel out on its first headlining tour. The group also served as its own setup and teardown crew.

“We set up all the stage design, lighting, all the booths that we had,” Plank said, calling it a boots-on-the-ground experiment and, unexpectedly, a bonding one.

What Shuffit remembers is the singing.

“We were filling a room with young adults and people from all age groups and doing like two hours of worship, only playing our songs,” he said. “Me and Chelsea have both been a part of SEU Worship long enough to know that there were times in the early days where that wasn’t always possible. There wasn’t always a room full of people that could sing our songs.”

“That was a very sobering and humbling realization.”

The song he keeps coming back to isn’t the one Plank almost left off. It’s “Bless the Blood,” written in an unusually small room — just him, Plank and Caylie Bryant.

“We had to fight for it,” he said. Months of it, on and off: leaving it, coming back to it, leaving it, coming back to it. It wasn’t finished until the week of the recording.

“The way that it portrays the sacrifice that Christ made for us, and the power that that has, is some of the most moving lyrical content I’ve ever gotten to be a part of.”

As for the song she tried to leave behind, Plank has noticed where it lands hardest, and it isn’t with students. It’s with the people running things.

“Where I’ve seen it connecting specifically is with other church leaders,” she said. “Because of just remembering the why.”

“It’s just a joy to give up our lives for the Gospel.”

items.title: Why American Catholics Should Be Encouraged by JD Vance’s ‘Communion’
items.author: Dr. Richard DeClue
items.summary:
Dr. Richard DeClue

He is a politician who is taking Catholic social doctrine to heart. I think that is something that should encourage American Catholics, no matter their party affiliation.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

When I was an undergraduate theology major, I took a couple of courses that dealt with Catholic social doctrine. Prior to that, my only formation in things political and economic came from my environment as an American Gen Xer. In that milieu, politics was principally defined in binary terms: Democrat or Republican. For many, these labels were synonymous with good guys and bad guys (or vice versa). Reading the primary texts of papal magisterial teaching from Leo XIII’s Rerum Novarum to Pope St. John Paul II’s Centesimus Annus was a game-changer for me. (Note: I graduated college before the later encyclicals were promulgated.)

In those documents, I sensed a wisdom that transcended my twentieth/twenty-first-century American myopathy. The social encyclicals struck me as profoundly true. They also provided me a metric with which I could detect both good and bad aspects in the platforms of both ruling American political parties. Henceforth, my personal political and economic views were guided first and foremost by the principles outlined by Catholic social doctrine rather than by allegiance to any particular political party.

I did not expect to find similar sentiments and experiences presented in a book written by a sitting vice president. Yet here we are. While reading JD Vance’s recently published book, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, I was struck at the impact that Catholic social doctrine had on the vice president’s conversion and political perspective. In fact, Chapter 8 is entitled “Of New Things,” which is an English translation of the aforementioned encyclical by Pope Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum. I certainly did not expect to see a Republican political figure approvingly describe its teaching, which, as Vance writes, “forcefully advocates for the rights of individual workers, for labor unions” (153) and “lays out a vision of society where the state protects the vulnerable, guarantees a just wage for laborers, and ensures that working people have sufficient ‘rest from labor’” (154).

That’s a far cry from the quasi-idolatry some conservatives pay to the supposedly all-powerful, perfectly just “free market” economy. (Of course, Catholic social doctrine affirms the positive values of properly regulated capitalism, but it rejects the notion that an absolutely free market system will, by itself, guarantee economic justice.) It is also quite far from conservative commentator William F. Buckley, Jr.’s public criticism of Pope St. John XXIII’s social encyclical, Mater et Magistra (Mother and Teacher), expressed with the quip: “mater si, magistra no” (“mother yes, teacher no”).

Conservative commentator, Ben Shapiro, was also surprised—but not in a good way—by Vance’s book and related comments Vance made on The Joe Rogan Experience. Shapiro expressed concern that Vance’s views were too close to those of Democrats concerning economic oversight. One of his criticisms is that Vance’s book advocates too much for Catholic social doctrine. He seems to think that doing so would turn American economic policy into some sort of socialist state.

However, as Vance notes, Rerum Novarum “is critical of socialism” (154). In fact, as Leo XIII’s firmly states, “It is clear that the main tenant of socialism, community of goods, must be utterly rejected, since it only injures those whom it would seem meant to benefit, is directly contrary to the natural rights of mankind, and would introduce confusion and disorder into the commonweal” (Rerum Novarum 15). Marxism, socialism, and communism are repeatedly repudiated by Catholic social doctrine.

But pure laissez-faire capitalism and forms of Marxism are not the only options. As Vance describes Catholic social doctrine: “It is neither conservative nor progressive; neither liberal nor authoritarian” (154). In Centesimus Annus, Pope St. John Paul II asks whether “capitalism should be the goal of the countries now making efforts to rebuild their economy and society” (42). His answer is as follows:

If by “capitalism” is meant an economic system which recognizes the fundamental and positive role of business, the market, private property and the resulting responsibility for the means of production, as well as free human creativity in the economic sector, then the answer is certainly in the affirmative. . . . But if by “capitalism” is meant a system in which freedom in the economic sector is not circumscribed within a strong juridical framework which places it at the service of human freedom in its totality, and which sees it as a particular aspect of that freedom, the core of which is ethical and religious, then the reply is certainly negative.

In other words, capitalism can be an appropriate means of running a nation’s economy, so long as economics is not seen as the only or supreme value to which all else is subordinated. Economics that ought to be subordinated to higher principles and values.

For example, just because a worker is willing to accept a low wage due to a lack of better alternative options does not mean the low wage is just. To this point, see the teaching of Rerum Novarum 45:

Let the working man and the employer make free agreements, and in particular let them agree freely as to the wages; nevertheless, there underlies a dictate of natural justice more imperious and ancient than any bargain between man and man, namely, that wages ought not to be insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved wage-earner. If through necessity or fear of a worse evil the workman [were to] accept harder conditions because an employer or contractor will afford him no better, he is made the victim of force and injustice.

JD Vance quotes this very passage in his book (155). Similar principles apply to working hours and conditions. Workers are to be afforded sufficient time to spend with their families, for their healthy recuperation via rest, and most especially to be able to worship God (see Rerum Novarum 41–42). 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Humans are not just wealth-generating machines; they are persons endowed with dignity, whose well-being must be respected. “Pope Leo XIII’s theory of human nature,” writes Vance, “strikes a balance so perfect it seems divinely inspired” (156). In this way, Catholic social doctrine was a significant element in JD Vance’s conversion to Catholicism, as Bishop Barron has noted.

I’ve only been able to highlight a few aspects of this complex topic as it is treated in Vance’s book. Much more could be said, including his chapter on “A Dismal Science” (i.e., economics). I could also highlight many of the other aspects of Catholicism that JD Vance found compelling and attractive. I highlight these issues, precisely because he is a politician who is taking Catholic social doctrine to heart. I think that is something that should encourage American Catholics, no matter their party affiliation.

Because he is a Republican, those Catholic Democrats who are predisposed to dislike anyone from across the aisle might not be willing to take that seriously. I think that would be a mistake. Too often, Catholics on either side of the political divide lob accusations at each other, usually by pointing out those aspects of Catholic teaching that the other party seems to flounder on. However, I think Catholics should be willing to laud members of the other party when they exhibit a willingness to be led by Catholic doctrine, especially in instances when they are seen as going against their own party’s standard line of thought.

I would hope that if a prominent Democrat politician were to discuss the role of the Church’s Pro-Life doctrine as a major element of their conversion to Catholicism that Catholic Republicans would applaud them. Even if a non-Catholic Democrat came out as actively Pro-Life, I hope Republicans would voice public support for that stance.

In our politically divided times, perhaps that’s naive. But I hope not. While I am not saying that every Catholic must agree with everything that JD Vance has said or advocated for in the book or elsewhere, I would like to suggest that there is much in his conversion story that ought to encourage us as fellow American Catholics. In short: Democrat Catholics should be grateful that a Republican is sharing some of their long-held values; Republican Catholics should be grateful that a Republican is addressing some of their party’s historic weaknesses. All Catholics should be grateful that a man who once lost his Christian faith found it again, this time within the Catholic Church.

items.title: Faith in the Shadow of the Uncanny Valley: Matthew Gasda’s ‘Stranger Beauty’
items.author: Katy Carl
items.summary:
Katy Carl

The novel helps us to see is the nature of our moment’s carefully poised illusion, the shape of the bubble we live inside. It doesn't show what will remain when it pops.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Katy Carl

Most novels provide a sense of unity by means of illusion. What seems to be one story is actually at least two stories and often more. At the minimum level of complexity, we have a foreground story—the immediate action—and a background story, which helps to illumine and deepen and interpret the events that are unfolding in the narrative present. The newest offering from Matthew Gasda, Stranger Beauty, follows this predictable pattern to unpredictable places. 

The point-of-view protagonist, M, a retired but still young playwright, inhabits a technodystopia in the year 2038. The problem of mortality has been solved (at least for the well-off and at least in cities), and AI models oversee and optimize all the most intimate day-to-day logistics. The drama of life is now not whether the body will survive but whether the spirit will. Shorn of purpose, M meditates on the sources of his current life and finds at least one of their taproots back in the year 2023, in the pages of old journals he kept while making the decisions whose consequences he now lives. 

The journals plunge the reader into a quasi-hypnotic, aphoristic meditation on the continuity of human identity over time, while the 2038 foreground plot develops into a timely examination of the nature of human creativity against so-called AI “generativity.” The flashes of epiphany are called into question by the final outcome, and that outcome implicitly asks: Is this “newer thing,” the machine simulacrum of consciousness, simply one more feature of the world outside our heads? Is it a beneficent presence seeking entrance and hospitality, one to which we owe xenia, welcome of the stranger? Or is it instead a Trojan horse, leviathan, panopticon, Chthulu, Dave, Borg: a dream-monster we must either evade or slay before it eats us alive in the name of a false communion?

Much has already been said of this, and most readers’ sentiments will be entrenched in one camp or another. By placing his foreground action in the future, Gasda skillfully threads the needle so that readers will have to face not our own present situation but that of a possible, and for now counterfactual, future. 

That narrative strategy effects another skillful and necessary evasion too: Because of Gasda’s prior success as a playwright, whatever he writes is far too often interpreted by commentators as though it were some kind of skeleton key for a scene, a social movement, or even a generation. Here I intend to ignore, just as Gasda bypasses, that noisy yet nebulous context and take this work on its own conceptual and technical terms. It becomes easier to do this with Stranger Beauty than with any of his previous works because for once Gasda is writing not about “the moment” but about whatever in the human is also timeless. 

As Daniel McInerny observes in Beauty and Imitation, “One of the chief ways a culture puts its customs into question is through storytelling.” It will be news to precisely no one reading this piece that, in our time, technologically sophisticated humanity stands in conflicted relation to its own biology. Gasda picks up on this conflict and profoundly puts it into question, especially where the conflict cuts across relationships between men and women. A preoccupation with human generativity, in both the physical and spiritual senses, pervades the plot. Sexuality is therefore inescapably present. Yet in contrast to Gasda’s previous novel The Sleepers, sexuality is presented here more implicitly and subtly, less explicitly and exhibitively. For this reason, many Christians—whose conceptual language Gasda’s protagonist freely borrows even as it remains unclear whether he counts himself one of them—may find this novel worth engaging. It will still strain the comfort zones of some, who others may consider its repetitious hints and whispers of skin and sense extraneous to the plot.

They are, however, not extraneous. What is revealed by these brief vignettes—glimpses rather than scenes—is not so much the compulsive and self-regarding nature of most nonmarital coupling (although that also comes to the surface). Still more, they presence the very real sense in which the “marital act” even prior to marriage or without intention of fidelity truly makes two one so that the subsequent uncoupling of their human concerns and questions becomes at best a bloodletting, at worst an irreducible impossibility. 

What stands out about Gasda’s treatment of this motif is that he gets to the heart of both the real sadness and real joy of eros and its irreducible orientation toward fruitfulness. Even though M and his then-girlfriend-now-wife, S—, or Sophia (“her name means gnosis”), do marry and raise a child together, by the time of the foreground (2038) action, their relationship has fallen apart. They remember the vivid frisson of their low-commitment days, yet they cannot recapture it under the current conditions of their life. These conditions, in turn, have less to do with the supposedly dulling effects of a vow of fidelity (M at one point confesses to a powerful, marrow-deep craving for stability) and far more to do with their technological, economic, and aesthetic milieu. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Gradually, it emerges that M has sold away his previous body of creative work to an AI company to train its models in exchange for dubious technodystopian benefits whose nature is only slowly and partially revealed. Gasda draws a direct, explicit parallel between M’s creative impotence and its literal, physical analogue following this decision. Sophia, as a spouse, remains compelling and continues to long vocally for her husband; she, it’s implied, is flourishing from the effects of life-extension treatments that may also be, to some extent, the cause of M’s malaise; but, again, the bodiliness—or disembodiment—of their connection is not incidental to the story. It is key to understanding what a machine is not and will never be. 

That important meditation is, unfortunately, not especially well served by the choppy, aphoristic form which the novel’s extended middle section is delivered. These shard-like reflections are taken from M’s secret journals which themselves echo, probably on purpose, Gasda’s own “Writer’s Diary” available both on Substack and in print form.

Often incisive as observations and frequently freighted with important detail whose disclosure affects how, the diaristic sections nevertheless carry less weight as fictional rendering because they are so fragmentary and so disconnected from the moments of embodied life that promoted them. The reader is not always given to understand, even, whether the sensory stimuli they describe are being experienced, remembered, or merely imagined. 

That is to say, these aphorisms are already to some extent mechanized, and M’s jealously guarding them from the machine—the only part of his oeuvre he didn’t sell in his Faustian deal—may be superfluous, too little too late. 

To be clear, this is not a criticism of the “Diary” itself, which provides minute slices of thought and experience that, in themselves, are often quite compelling. I follow the “Writer’s Diary” avidly and often find individual lines sympathetic or illuminating, but when transposed wholesale and at great length into novelistic structure, their form can’t fully deliver the integrated texture of sustained experience that narrative prose requires in order to produce a full, willing suspension of disbelief. The reader remains alert to the man behind the curtain, positioning M, Sophia, Ruby, Kairos, and their other connections and contacts in tableaux vivants from which the sense of imminent movement, meaningful action, only intermittently emerges. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

This effect of the dis-integration of form may be deliberate, as it puts the fictional M in a weaker position characterologically to oppose or resist the encompassing forces that bear in upon him. If deliberate, though, it must be noted that this choice results in the rendering of a character who constantly tells us we must resist disembodiment and dehumanization but who cannot show us what an effective resistance would look like. In itself, this is not objectionable. The fates of fictional protagonists only sometimes suggest models for action; other times, they imply warnings of danger. But if M offers a warning, it is a particularly hopeless one, suggesting that if even this protagonist with all his privileges is incapable of putting up a decent fight, no more will we be. If it is a promise of future technovitalist glory, it does not make that glory more appealing. 

 The novel’s concluding sequence, hypnotic and nearly hallucinatory, raises central questions of what is real and what is illusory, even as, despite flashes of gorgeousness, its overall effect lacks coherence. This decoherence, too, may be purposeful, though it is disorienting. Perhaps we ought to feel disoriented; we ought to notice our disorientation. We ought to realize that we are, like M, “mangled by the digital machinery [we] both use and [are] used by.” Maybe that is the point. 

A novel like this one has a value for its ability to provoke awareness: awareness of the perilous deciding moment that may already have passed; awareness of the self’s inevitable conflicts over how to meet what comes next. It is also interesting for its willingness to stretch our sense of what counts as, or belongs in, “a novel.” In art, experimentation drives forward and pushes the limits of what we can possibly say, but sometimes it does so at the risk of saying nothing or of committing fruitless self-contradictions. Ambiguous art can confound our shallow, unexamined expectations; it can demand reflection on realities we may otherwise feel hesitant to own; it can just as easily lead us into a labyrinth out of which there is no independent exit, only rescue. 

The productive disorientation found in Stranger Beauty reveals the counterproductive confounding, the confusion of identity, that lies at the heart of the problematic ethics of AI use in creative contexts: Is the “speaker,” “Kairos,” a real machine model speaking for an invented character (M) who mirrors the real artist (Gasda)? Or an invented machine voicing the invented character (M) who perhaps speaks, or perhaps does not speak, for the real artist? Gasda’s mimesis of our habit of naming our machines raises further questions still: Does the chosen name, Kairos, indicate that the machine aspires to guide us toward transcendence—or that it usurps our capacity for transcendence? 

The text does not provide definitive indications. The plot’s conclusion could be thought to support either answer, or both. Perhaps we need this ambiguity, this invitation to read against the grain so completely that we may have to ask which way the grain even runs in the first place. Perhaps it is necessary. For excellent narrative art often does not so much steer us toward a definitive set of answers so much as it provides us with substance and space to pose needed questions more articulately. This chameleonic shifting, this ability to reflect one facet of truth and now another without committing to any interpretation of either, has its merits, if limited ones. 

And yet, and yet—I think, now and often, of an assertion made by a minor character toward the end of Joshua Hren’s novel Infinite Regress. Observing the life of another character who cannot free himself from the différance of an endless recursive loop of self-questioning questions, this character pronounces that his intellectual friend has not in truth attained enlightenment but only a bijou residence inside a “small and shitty hell.” By deferring meaning and decision endlessly, this minor character (like so many other souls caught in the digital flotsam) drifts around and around a tantalizing lazy river, constantly thirsting for the water of life but never able to find a drink, forever asking “What is truth?” but never able to arrive at the True. Maybe Gasda, too, by letting us watch M ride around and around his own lazy river of rumination and reflection (and regret?), wants to bring his readers to that point of utter abandonment where we must demand a decisive answer or be lost entirely. Maybe.

But is this not becoming a pileup of too many maybes? In all this shipwreck of bodies and meanings, the reader may be forgiven for asking, as Hopkins asked over another wreck: Where, where was a, where was a place?

This is why I mean it as only ambiguous praise when I say that the last words of Gasda’s novel leave behind a haunting and apparently deliberate uncertainty. Today’s intellectuals have, for the most part, been trained to desire and expect inconclusive conclusions in the name of openness: not to be, as Girard says repeatedly in A Theatre of Envy, naively “taken in by representation.” The ending of Stranger Beauty rightly refuses readers the comfort of superficial interpretations, sparks the desire to cling to what remains deeply valid when fluidity reigns and appearances deceive, and yet offers no hint of where to seek a compass for the search. 

The truth Stranger Beauty helps us to see, then, is just the nature of our moment’s carefully poised illusion, the shape of the bubble we all now live inside. What it does not show us, what perhaps no novel can show us, is what will remain stable when that bubble inevitably pops.
